To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the translocation dynamics of flexible polyelectrytes through a solid-state pore can be controlled by placing alternate charged-uncharged sections along the pore length, with an optimum section length that is independent of the polyelectroleyte and pore lengths.

(i) The translocation dynamics of polyelectroltytes through solid-state nanopores is affected by the charge pattern along the pore, (ii) The translocation time is maximum for a charge pattern with an optimal section length, (iii) This optimal section length is independent on the length of polyelectoltye or nanopore, (iv) The theory based on Fokker-Plank formalism is found in good agreement with the simulation data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the charge pattern along a solid state nanopore on the translocation time of a polyelectroelyte.
understanding the effect of charge patterns along nanopores on the translocation dynamics of flexible polyelectroltyes.
the effect of charge patterns along the pore on translocation dynamics, with an aim to understand the role of the charge distribution in the pore.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the translocation dynamics of the polymer can be controlled by varying the charge pattern along the solid-state nanopore.
charge patterns along a pore can be used to control the polyelectrolysate translocation through a nanopore, which is of immense importance in the context of single molecule sequencing.
the effect of charge patterns is to delay the translocation process and the delay is the largest for an optimum section length.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the charge pattern along a solid-state pore is an effective tool for controlling polyelectroelyte translocation dynamics.
the translocation dynamics of polyelectroltyes is not only dependent on the pore length but also on the pattern of charges along the pore.
the charge pattern along a solid state nanopore can be used for tuning the translocation dynamics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a nanopore patterned with alternate charged and unchared segments of optimum length can be used as an efficient filter to control the translocation of a polyelectroleyte.
the polyelectrolys can be slowed down in the pore ejection phase by placing alternate charged/uncharged sections along the pore.
the translocation time of a flexible charged polyelectrolysate through a nanopore can be controlled by varying the distribution of charges along the nanopore.
